221		// Track branch tips already pushed to the target so subsequent branches
222		// can advertise them as haves. Without this, the second branch in a
223		// multi-branch bootstrap re-sends all shared objects (e.g., linux's
224		// master and nocache-cleanup share ~99% of history).
225		completedRefs := planner.CopyRefHashMap(p.TargetRefs)
226	
227		for _, batch := range batches {
228			if batch.subsumed {
229				cmds := []gitproto.PushCommand{{
230					Name: batch.Plan.TargetRef,
231					Old:  plumbing.ZeroHash,
232					New:  batch.Plan.SourceHash,
233				}}
234				if err := p.TargetPusher.PushCommands(ctx, cmds); err != nil {
235					return result, fmt.Errorf("create subsumed branch ref for %s: %w", batch.Plan.TargetRef, err)
236				}
237				completedRefs[batch.Plan.TargetRef] = batch.Plan.SourceHash
238				result.BatchCount++
239				p.log("bootstrap batch subsumed branch finalized",
240					"branch", batch.Plan.TargetRef.String(),
241					"source_hash", planner.ShortHash(batch.Plan.SourceHash))
242				continue
243			}
244			result.PlannedBatchCount += len(batch.Checkpoints)
245			result.TempRefs = append(result.TempRefs, batch.TempRef.String())
246			p.log("bootstrap batch branch plan",
247				"branch", batch.Plan.TargetRef.String(),
248				"temp_ref", batch.TempRef.String(),
249				"planned_batches", len(batch.Checkpoints),
250				"resume_hash", planner.ShortHash(batch.ResumeHash))
251	
252			current := batch.ResumeHash
253			startIdx, err := planner.BootstrapResumeIndex(batch.Checkpoints, batch.ResumeHash)
254			if err != nil && !batch.ResumeHash.IsZero() && len(batch.chain) > 0 {
255				// Temp ref doesn't match any planned checkpoint (e.g., the user
256				// changed --target-max-pack-bytes between runs). If the hash is
257				// in the commit chain, reuse it as the starting point and re-plan
258				// remaining checkpoints — preserving already-pushed data.
259				if chainIdx := chainPosition(batch.chain, batch.ResumeHash); chainIdx >= 0 {
260					remaining := batch.chain[chainIdx+1:]
261					if len(remaining) > 0 {
262						numBatches := estimateBatchCount(int64(len(remaining)), p.TargetMaxPack)
263						batch.Checkpoints = evenCheckpoints(remaining, numBatches)
264						p.log("bootstrap batch resuming from stale temp ref",
265							"branch", batch.Plan.TargetRef.String(),
266							"resume_hash", planner.ShortHash(batch.ResumeHash),
267							"remaining_commits", len(remaining),
268							"new_batches", len(batch.Checkpoints))
269						startIdx = 0
270						err = nil
271					}
272				}
273			}
274			if err != nil && !batch.ResumeHash.IsZero() {
275				// Temp ref hash not in the chain at all — truly stale. Delete and start fresh.
276				p.log("bootstrap batch clearing stale temp ref",
277					"branch", batch.Plan.TargetRef.String(),
278					"temp_ref", batch.TempRef.String(),
279					"stale_hash", planner.ShortHash(batch.ResumeHash))
280				delCmds := []gitproto.PushCommand{{Name: batch.TempRef, Old: batch.ResumeHash, Delete: true}}
281				if delErr := p.TargetPusher.PushCommands(ctx, delCmds); delErr != nil {
282					return result, fmt.Errorf("delete stale temp ref %s: %w (original: %w)", batch.TempRef, delErr, err)
283				}
284				current = plumbing.ZeroHash
285				startIdx = 0
286			}
287	
288			// Manual index loop: subdivide may insert checkpoints at the current
289			// index, so we must not auto-increment after a retry.
290			idx := startIdx
291			for idx < len(batch.Checkpoints) {
292				checkpoint := batch.Checkpoints[idx]
293				p.log("bootstrap batch push checkpoint",
294					"branch", batch.Plan.TargetRef.String(),
295					"batch", idx+1,
296					"batch_total", len(batch.Checkpoints),
297					"from", planner.ShortHash(current),
298					"to", planner.ShortHash(checkpoint))
299	
300				stagePlans := []planner.BranchPlan{{
301					Branch: batch.Plan.Branch, SourceRef: batch.Plan.SourceRef,
302					TargetRef: batch.TempRef, SourceHash: checkpoint, TargetHash: current,
303					Kind: batch.Plan.Kind, Action: planner.ActionForTargetHash(current),
304					Reason: fmt.Sprintf("%s -> %s via %s", planner.ShortHash(current), planner.ShortHash(checkpoint), batch.TempRef),
305				}}
306				if idx == len(batch.Checkpoints)-1 {
307					stagePlans = append(stagePlans, planner.BranchPlan{
308						Branch: batch.Plan.Branch, SourceRef: batch.Plan.SourceRef,
309						TargetRef: batch.Plan.TargetRef, SourceHash: checkpoint,
310						TargetHash: plumbing.ZeroHash, Kind: batch.Plan.Kind,
311						Action: planner.ActionCreate,
312						Reason: fmt.Sprintf("create %s at %s", batch.Plan.TargetRef, planner.ShortHash(checkpoint)),
313					})
314				}
315	
316				packReader, err := packReaderForCheckpoint(ctx, p, batch, checkpoint, current, completedRefs, fetchLimit)
317				if err != nil {
318					return result, fmt.Errorf("fetch source batch pack for %s: %w", batch.Plan.TargetRef, err)
319				}
320				packReader = closeOnce(packReader)
321	
322				// Peek at the PACK header (12 bytes) to get the object count.
323				// If the estimated pack size exceeds the batch limit, subdivide
324				// immediately instead of pushing a pack the target will reject.
325				// This avoids wasting a multi-GiB transfer on a doomed push.
326				if p.TargetMaxPack > 0 && len(batch.chain) > 0 {
327					subdivided := false
328					packReader, err = checkPackSizeAndSubdivide(packReader, p.TargetMaxPack, func() bool {
329						expanded := subdivideCheckpoints(batch.chain, current, batch.Checkpoints[idx:])
330						if len(expanded) > len(batch.Checkpoints[idx:]) {
331							p.log("bootstrap batch subdividing before push (pack header estimate)",
332								"branch", batch.Plan.TargetRef.String(),
333								"old_remaining", len(batch.Checkpoints[idx:]),
334								"new_remaining", len(expanded))
335							batch.Checkpoints = append(batch.Checkpoints[:idx], expanded...)
336							subdivided = true
337							return true
338						}
339						return false
340					})
341					if err != nil {
342						return result, fmt.Errorf("check pack size for %s: %w", batch.Plan.TargetRef, err)
343					}
344					if subdivided {
345						continue // retry at same idx with new (smaller) checkpoint
346					}
347				}
348	
349				cmds := convert.PlansToPushCommands(stagePlans)
350				if err := p.TargetPusher.PushPack(ctx, cmds, packReader); err != nil {
351					_ = packReader.Close()
352					if isTargetBodyLimitError(err) && len(batch.chain) > 0 {
353						expanded := subdivideCheckpoints(batch.chain, current, batch.Checkpoints[idx:])
354						if len(expanded) > len(batch.Checkpoints[idx:]) {
355							p.log("bootstrap batch subdividing after target size rejection",
356								"branch", batch.Plan.TargetRef.String(),
357								"old_remaining", len(batch.Checkpoints[idx:]),
358								"new_remaining", len(expanded),
359								"error", err.Error())
360							batch.Checkpoints = append(batch.Checkpoints[:idx], expanded...)
361							continue // retry at same idx with new (smaller) checkpoint
362						}
363					}
364					return result, fmt.Errorf("push bootstrap batch for %s: %w", batch.Plan.TargetRef, err)
365				}
366				_ = packReader.Close()
367				p.log("bootstrap batch checkpoint complete",
368					"branch", batch.Plan.TargetRef.String(),
369					"batch", idx+1,
370					"batch_total", len(batch.Checkpoints))
371				current = checkpoint
372				result.BatchCount++
373				idx++
374			}
375	
376			if current.IsZero() {
377				return result, fmt.Errorf("bootstrap batching for %s completed with no checkpoint state", batch.Plan.TargetRef)
378			}
379			if batch.ResumeHash == batch.Plan.SourceHash && p.TargetRefs[batch.Plan.TargetRef].IsZero() {
380				cmds := []gitproto.PushCommand{{Name: batch.Plan.TargetRef, Old: plumbing.ZeroHash, New: batch.Plan.SourceHash}}
381				if err := p.TargetPusher.PushCommands(ctx, cmds); err != nil {
382					return result, fmt.Errorf("resume bootstrap cutover for %s: %w", batch.Plan.TargetRef, err)
383				}
384			}
385	
386			cmds := []gitproto.PushCommand{{Name: batch.TempRef, Old: current, Delete: true}}
387			if err := p.TargetPusher.PushCommands(ctx, cmds); err != nil {
388				return result, fmt.Errorf("delete bootstrap temp ref for %s: %w", batch.Plan.TargetRef, err)
389			}
```

Both are addressable. Let me lay out the plan, then implement:

**Point 1 — rate keeps "rotting" after transfer ends.** The rate is `bytes / (now − start)`, so once bytes stop flowing, dividing by an ever-growing wall clock makes it shrink. Fix: track a per-side `lastByteAt` timestamp on every `Read`, compute the rate as `bytes / (lastByteAt − start)`. The number freezes at the actual transfer rate. Plus, append a `✓` marker once a side has been idle for >750ms so it's visually obvious.

**Point 2 — show current packfile during batched bootstrap.** The bootstrap loop already knows `batch idx+1 / total` and currently logs it (bootstrap.go:293). I'll add a `phase` field to the stats collector with a setter, plumb a callback through `bootstrap.Params`, and the progress renderer suffixes the line with `(pack 3/8)`.

I'll do these as two separate commits. Starting with point 1.

  "new_string": "// liveSides returns a snapshot of per-side byte totals for live rendering.\n// ActiveNanos and IdleNanos are computed against time.Now() at snapshot\n// time so callers do not need to know the collector's start instant.\nfunc (s *statsCollector) liveSides() []SideBytes {\n\ts.sidesMu.RLock()\n\tdefer s.sidesMu.RUnlock()\n\tstartNanos := s.startedAt.UnixNano()\n\tnowNanos := time.Now().UnixNano()\n\tout := make([]SideBytes, 0, len(s.sides))\n\tfor label, sc := range s.sides {\n\t\tbytes := sc.bytes.Load()\n\t\tlastByte := sc.lastByteAt.Load()\n\t\tvar activeNanos, idleNanos int64\n\t\tif lastByte > 0 {\n\t\t\tactiveNanos = lastByte - startNanos\n\t\t\tif activeNanos < 0 {\n\t\t\t\tactiveNanos = 0\n\t\t\t}\n\t\t\tidleNanos = nowNanos - lastByte\n\t\t\tif idleNanos < 0 {\n\t\t\t\tidleNanos = 0\n\t\t\t}\n\t\t}\n\t\tout = append(out, SideBytes{\n\t\t\tLabel:       label,\n\t\t\tBytes:       bytes,\n\t\t\tDisplay:     sc.display,\n\t\t\tActiveNanos: activeNanos,\n\t\t\tIdleNanos:   idleNanos,\n\t\t})\n\t}\n\treturn out\n}"
}

{
  "command": "git add -A && git commit -m \"$(cat <<'EOF'\nFreeze per-side rate once a transfer goes idle\n\nPreviously the rate displayed in the --progress ticker and the\nend-of-run throughput line was computed as bytes / (now − start),\nwhich kept shrinking once bytes stopped flowing — a sync that\nstreamed 11 MB at 367 KB/s would tick down to 366, 365, 364 ... while\nthe post-transfer phases (planning, ref creation) ran. Misleading.\n\nTrack per-side lastByteAt on every non-empty Read and surface two\nnew fields on each SideBytes snapshot: ActiveNanos (start → last\nbyte) and IdleNanos (last byte → snapshot time). Renderers compute\nthe rate from ActiveNanos so it freezes at the actual transfer\nrate, and append a \"✓\" marker once IdleNanos crosses 750ms (or\nunconditionally on the final render) so it's visually obvious which\nsides have finished.\nEOF\n)\" 2>&1 | tail -3",
  "description": "Commit point 1"
}

> AGENT

Both shipped:

**Point 1 (`ed2dd56`)** — Rate now freezes at the active-window value (`bytes / (lastByteAt − start)`) instead of decaying as wall clock keeps moving past the last byte. Once a side has been idle for >750ms it gets a `✓` marker. The final frame force-marks all sides. So your earlier transfer would now read e.g. `github.com → 11.3 MB @ 367 KB/s ✓  │  11.3 MB @ 366 KB/s ✓ → cloudflare.net` and stay there during the post-transfer ref-creation phase.

**Point 2 (`6fcd650`)** — Bootstrap publishes its current activity through a new `OnPhase` callback on `bstrap.Params`. The renderer reads it and appends `(pack 3/8)` to live frames. Covers all three bootstrap shapes:
- one-shot: `(pushing pack)`
- batched checkpoints: `(pack N/M)` per checkpoint
- post-batch tag push: `(pushing tags)`

The phase suffix is suppressed on the final frame so it doesn't read as still-running.

Try a real run with a chunky repo and you should see the pack counter advancing while the target rate is active, then both sides settling with `✓` once the dust clears.

- `refs/heads/feat/checkpoints-v2-validation`

So this is just a typo / wrong name — the planner correctly threw "no source refs matched" because nothing on source is called that.

That said, looking at this output reveals two genuinely useful UX things we *could* improve:

1. **Better error.** "no source refs matched" is terse. We could add: "requested branches: `entire/checkpoints/v1`; available: `main`, `entire-activity`, `entire/trails/v1`, …" so a typo is obvious without dropping into `git ls-remote`.

2. **Suggest near-matches.** When the user asks for `entire/checkpoints/v1` and we see `entire/trails/v1` exists, we could surface that explicitly.

Want me to land #1? It's a 5-line change in the planner — useful in the same scenario you just hit, and unrelated to the progress work so easy to keep separate.

  "new_string": "// humanBytes renders a byte count in IEC-ish binary units. Local copy\n// because importing the syncer's formatter would invert the dependency\n// direction; the bootstrap package is meant to be standalone.\nfunc humanBytes(n int64) string {\n\tconst unit = 1024\n\tif n < unit {\n\t\treturn fmt.Sprintf(\"%d B\", n)\n\t}\n\tdiv, exp := int64(unit), 0\n\tfor x := n / unit; x >= unit; x /= unit {\n\t\tdiv *= unit\n\t\texp++\n\t}\n\tvalue := float64(n) / float64(div)\n\tsuffix := []string{\"KB\", \"MB\", \"GB\", \"TB\", \"PB\"}[exp]\n\tif value >= 100 {\n\t\treturn fmt.Sprintf(\"%.0f %s\", value, suffix)\n\t}\n\tif value >= 10 {\n\t\treturn fmt.Sprintf(\"%.1f %s\", value, suffix)\n\t}\n\treturn fmt.Sprintf(\"%.2f %s\", value, suffix)\n}\n\nfunc isTargetBodyLimitError(err error) bool {"
}

> AGENT

Done. Re-running your big sync, when bootstrap goes from 1 → 2 → 4 packs you'd now see something like:

```
target rejected pack — splitting 1 → 2 packs
github.com → 1.63 GB @ 5.17 MB/s  │  1.63 GB @ 5.16 MB/s → cloudflare.net  (pack 1/2)
target rejected pack — splitting 2 → 4 packs
github.com → 1.63 GB @ 5.17 MB/s  │  1.63 GB @ 5.16 MB/s → cloudflare.net  (pack 1/4)
```

Three triggers now produce notices:
- `target rejected pack — switching to batched mode (limit 512 MB)` — when the very first one-shot push gets refused and we fall back to batched
- `pack would exceed target limit — splitting N → M packs` — when the pre-push header estimate already shows the pack is too big
- `target rejected pack — splitting N → M packs` — when the actual push gets rejected (your case)

When `--progress` is off, the notices fall through to plain stderr so the information isn't lost.

670	
671	// estimatedBytesPerObject is a conservative average for compressed git objects
672	// in a packfile. Used with the PACK header's object count to estimate total
673	// pack size before streaming the full pack. Real values range from ~200 bytes
674	// (tiny commits in a sparse repo) to ~2 KiB (blob-heavy repos), with most
675	// mature repos averaging 500–1000 bytes. 750 is a reasonable middle ground.
676	const estimatedBytesPerObject = 750
677	
678	// checkPackSizeAndSubdivide reads the 12-byte PACK header to get the object
679	// count, estimates total pack size, and if it exceeds batchLimit, closes the
680	// reader and calls subdivide(). Returns (nil, nil) when subdivided (caller
681	// should continue to retry), or (prepended reader, nil) to proceed with push.
682	func checkPackSizeAndSubdivide(
683		r io.ReadCloser,
684		batchLimit int64,
685		subdivide func() bool,
686	) (io.ReadCloser, error) { //nolint:unparam // error return kept for future use
687		var header [12]byte
688		n, err := io.ReadFull(r, header[:])
689		if err != nil {
690			// Short pack or error — let the push handle it
691			prefixed := io.MultiReader(bytes.NewReader(header[:n]), r)
692			return &wrappedMultiRC{Reader: prefixed, Closer: r}, nil //nolint:nilerr // below threshold is not an error, we return the original reader
693		}
694		if string(header[:4]) != "PACK" {
695			// Not a standard packfile — can't estimate, proceed
696			prefixed := io.MultiReader(bytes.NewReader(header[:]), r)
697			return &wrappedMultiRC{Reader: prefixed, Closer: r}, nil
698		}
699		objectCount := int64(header[8])<<24 | int64(header[9])<<16 | int64(header[10])<<8 | int64(header[11])
700		estimated := objectCount * estimatedBytesPerObject
701	
702		if estimated > batchLimit && subdivide() {
703			_ = r.Close()
704			return nil, nil //nolint:nilnil // nil reader signals no subdivision needed
705		}
706	
707		prefixed := io.MultiReader(bytes.NewReader(header[:]), r)
708		return &wrappedMultiRC{Reader: prefixed, Closer: r}, nil
709	}
710	
711	type wrappedMultiRC struct {
712		io.Reader
713		io.Closer
714	}
715	
716	func (w *wrappedMultiRC) Read(p []byte) (int, error) {
717		n, err := w.Reader.Read(p)
718		if err != nil && !errors.Is(err, io.EOF) {
719			return n, fmt.Errorf("read prepended pack: %w", err)
720		}
721		return n, err //nolint:wrapcheck // io.EOF must not be wrapped to preserve io.Reader contract
722	}
723	
724	// chainPosition returns the index of hash in chain, or -1 if not found.
725	func chainPosition(chain []plumbing.Hash, hash plumbing.Hash) int {
726		for i, h := range chain {
727			if h == hash {
728				return i
729			}
730		}
731		return -1
732	}
733	
734	// subdivideCheckpoints splits each remaining checkpoint range in half using
735	// the full commit chain. Called when a batch push is rejected for exceeding
736	// the target's body-size limit. Returns the expanded checkpoint list; if no
737	// split is possible (ranges are already 1 commit), returns the input unchanged.
738	func subdivideCheckpoints(chain []plumbing.Hash, current plumbing.Hash, remaining []plumbing.Hash) []plumbing.Hash {
739		chainIdx := make(map[plumbing.Hash]int, len(chain))
740		for i, h := range chain {
741			chainIdx[h] = i
742		}
743		curIdx, ok := chainIdx[current]
744		if !ok && !current.IsZero() {
745			return remaining
746		}
747		if current.IsZero() {
748			curIdx = -1
749		}

Now your subdivision notices carry actual numbers. For your earlier sync the sequence would read like:

```
estimated pack ~3.4 GB exceeds target limit 512 MB — splitting 1 → 2 packs (~1.7 GB each)
github.com → 1.63 GB @ 5.17 MB/s  │  1.63 GB @ 5.16 MB/s → cloudflare.net  (pack 1/2)
target rejected pack (target limit 256 MB) — splitting 2 → 4 packs
github.com → 1.63 GB @ 5.17 MB/s  │  1.63 GB @ 5.16 MB/s → cloudflare.net  (pack 1/4)
```

The pre-push estimate uses the actual PACK header object count × 750 bytes/object (already in the codebase). The post-rejection one parses the body limit out of the server error and falls back to a bare "target rejected pack" message if the limit isn't extractable. Per-pack estimates are `estimated_total / new_count` — slightly approximate since real distribution varies, but useful as a sanity check.

> AGENT

Actually no — your guess is half-right. Walk through what happened with the code as it stands:

1. **First push (one-shot)** failed with something that matched `isTargetBodyLimitError` — a 413, or text containing `body exceeded size limit` / `request body too large`. That's the only path that flips us into batched mode and sets `TargetMaxPack`. HTTP 500 alone wouldn't.

2. **Second push (batched, 1/2)** — once we're in batched mode, the *pre-push header estimate* takes over. It doesn't look at the server response at all; it just multiplies the PACK header's object count by 750 bytes/object and compares to `TargetMaxPack`. If the estimate exceeds the limit, it splits proactively — that's how 1 went to 2 and 2 went to 4 without anything actually being rejected.

3. **Push at 1/4** — header estimate now fits the limit, so we send the pack. Cloudflare returns HTTP 500 + `Internal Server Error`. Our `isTargetBodyLimitError` checks for `"body exceeded size limit"`, `"request body" + "too large"`, `"payload" + "too large"`, `"http 413"` — none of those match. So the post-rejection subdivide branch correctly *doesn't* trigger, the error propagates, and the sync dies.

So the code isn't shrinking *because of* the 500. The shrinking already happened earlier in the run from real body-size errors; the 500 at 1/4 is something else and we surface it cleanly.

That said, the 500 at 1/4 might still be Cloudflare's way of saying "too big" — they're inconsistent about it. Two genuinely useful fixes if you want to chase this:

- **Treat HTTP 500 from this Cloudflare endpoint as a body-size signal** (matches `Server=cloudflare` header + 5xx) and let it trigger another subdivide. Risky — it would also retry actual server bugs as size issues.
- **Add a max-subdivision guard** so we don't shrink forever if subdivisions stop helping. E.g., bail after N subdivisions of the same range with no progress.

Want me to look at the actual response body / headers next time it 500s by running a `curl` against that endpoint with a mock pack, or just add a `--verbose` slog line for each push attempt + status code so you can see the sequence directly? My recommendation: add the verbose log first, run once more, then we know whether to widen the body-limit heuristic.

> AGENT

A little, yes — `--verbose` already logs the high-level bootstrap events (fetching, pushing, subdividing, switching to batched), but it's missing two things that would actually answer "is Cloudflare's 500 a size issue":

1. **The estimated pack size at every push attempt** — we compute it in `checkPackSizeAndSubdivide` but only log it when we *do* subdivide. I'd log it on every push so you see the trajectory: `push attempt: ~600 MB → split`, then `push attempt: ~300 MB → split`, then `push attempt: ~150 MB → 500`. If that final 500 fires at 150 MB while the limit is 256 MB, it's almost certainly not a body-size issue. If it fires at 240 MB just under the 256 limit, Cloudflare is probably masking body-size as 500.

2. **The HTTP error from every failed push, not just the propagated final one.** Right now we only see the last error's body+headers because that's what gets returned. The intermediate ones that triggered subdivisions get logged with their `err.Error()` only on the subdivide path; if a push fails for some other reason in the middle of a batch we wouldn't see its details. Logging `err.Error()` (which already includes the Cf-Ray and response body) on the failure path before propagating would make the sequence transparent.

Both are 2-3 line additions in `internal/strategy/bootstrap/bootstrap.go` — no new infrastructure, just `p.log(...)` calls in the right places. Want me to land them so you can re-run with `--verbose` and we have actual data?

243	// progressSink returns a line-prefixing io.Writer suitable for
244	// sideband.Demuxer.Progress. When verbose is false it returns nil so the
245	// demuxer discards progress frames without allocating.
246	func progressSink(verbose bool, prefix string) io.Writer {
247		if !verbose {
248			return nil
249		}
250		return &prefixedLineWriter{w: os.Stderr, prefix: prefix, atLineStart: true}
251	}
252	
253	// prefixedLineWriter prepends a fixed prefix to each line of input written
254	// to the wrapped writer. Git sideband progress arrives as chunks that may
255	// contain '\n' between full lines or '\r' for in-place updates ("Resolving
256	// deltas:  12%\r"); both are treated as line terminators so the next chunk
257	// gets a fresh prefix.
258	type prefixedLineWriter struct {
259		w           io.Writer
260		prefix      string
261		atLineStart bool
262	}
263	
264	func (p *prefixedLineWriter) Write(b []byte) (int, error) {
265		consumed := 0
266		for len(b) > 0 {
267			if p.atLineStart {
268				if _, err := io.WriteString(p.w, p.prefix); err != nil {
269					return consumed, fmt.Errorf("write prefix: %w", err)
270				}
271				p.atLineStart = false
272			}
273			i := bytes.IndexAny(b, "\r\n")
274			var chunk []byte
275			if i < 0 {
276				chunk = b
277			} else {
278				chunk = b[:i+1]
279				p.atLineStart = true
280			}
281			n, err := p.w.Write(chunk)
282			consumed += n
283			if err != nil {
284				return consumed, fmt.Errorf("write chunk: %w", err)
285			}
286			b = b[len(chunk):]
287		}
288		return consumed, nil
289	}

251	func storeV2FetchPack(store storer.Storer, r io.Reader, verbose bool) error {
252		reader := NewPacketReader(r)
253		expectPackfile := false
254		for {
255			kind, payload, err := reader.ReadPacket()
256			if err != nil {
257				if errors.Is(err, io.EOF) {
258					if expectPackfile {
259						return errors.New("expected packfile to be sent after 'ready'")
260					}
261					return nil
262				}
263				return fmt.Errorf("decode protocol v2 fetch response: %w", err)

266			case PacketFlush:

271			case PacketDelim, PacketResponseEnd:
272				continue
273			case PacketData:

276					return errors.New("remote: " + line[4:])

278				switch line {
279				case "packfile\n":
280					demux := sideband.NewDemuxer(sideband.Sideband64k, reader.BufReader())

284					}
285					return nil
286				case "acknowledgments\n":
287					ready, err := skipV2Acknowledgments(reader)
288					if err != nil {
289						return err
290					}
291					expectPackfile = ready
292				case "shallow-info\n":
293					expectPackfile = true
294					if err := SkipSection(reader); err != nil {
295						return err
296					}
297				default:
298					return fmt.Errorf("unexpected protocol v2 fetch section %q", strings.TrimSpace(line))
299				}
300			}
301		}
302	}

156	func fetchToStoreV2(
157		ctx context.Context,
158		store storer.Storer,
159		conn *Conn,
160		caps *V2Capabilities,
161		desired map[plumbing.ReferenceName]DesiredRef,
162		targetRefs map[plumbing.ReferenceName]plumbing.Hash,
163		verbose bool,
164	) error {
165		wants := collectWants(desired)
166		haves := SortedUniqueHashes(refValues(targetRefs))
167		if len(wants) == 0 {
168			return git.NoErrAlreadyUpToDate
169		}
170	
171		cmdArgs := make([]string, 0, len(wants)+len(haves)+4)
172		// NOTE: no "thin-pack" argument. The relayed pack must stay
173		// self-contained so callers (e.g. replicate) can forward it to
174		// receive-pack servers that may advertise "no-thin". See
175		// planner.SupportsReplicateRelay for the matching invariant.
176		cmdArgs = append(cmdArgs, "ofs-delta")
177		if !verbose {
178			cmdArgs = append(cmdArgs, "no-progress")
179		}
180		for _, h := range wants {
181			cmdArgs = append(cmdArgs, "want "+h.String())
182		}
183		for _, h := range haves {
184			cmdArgs = append(cmdArgs, "have "+h.String())
185		}
186		cmdArgs = append(cmdArgs, "done")
187

489		}
490	
491		buffered := bufio.NewReader(reader)

494			_ = reader.Close()
495			return nil, fmt.Errorf("decode server response: %w", decErr)

498			_ = reader.Close()
499			return nil, fmt.Errorf("drain server response: %w", drainErr)

501		return &wrappedRC{
502			Reader: buildSidebandReader(caps, buffered, progressSink(verbose, "source: ")),
503			Closer: reader,
504		}, nil
505	}

200	func fetchPackV2(
201		ctx context.Context,
202		conn *Conn,
203		caps *V2Capabilities,
204		desired map[plumbing.ReferenceName]DesiredRef,
205		targetRefs map[plumbing.ReferenceName]plumbing.Hash,
206		verbose bool,
207	) (io.ReadCloser, error) {
208		wants := collectWants(desired)
209		haves := SortedUniqueHashes(refValues(targetRefs))
210		if len(wants) == 0 {
211			return nil, git.NoErrAlreadyUpToDate
212		}
213	
214		cmdArgs := make([]string, 0, len(wants)+len(haves)+4)
215		// NOTE: no "thin-pack" argument. The relayed pack must stay
216		// self-contained so callers (e.g. replicate) can forward it to
217		// receive-pack servers that may advertise "no-thin". See
218		// planner.SupportsReplicateRelay for the matching invariant.
219		cmdArgs = append(cmdArgs, "ofs-delta")
220		if !verbose {
221			cmdArgs = append(cmdArgs, "no-progress")
222		}
223		// Only request include-tag if the server supports it (issue #6).
224		if hasTag(desired) && caps.FetchSupports("include-tag") {
225			cmdArgs = append(cmdArgs, "include-tag")
226		}
227		for _, h := range wants {
228			cmdArgs = append(cmdArgs, "want "+h.String())
229		}
230		for _, h := range haves {
231			cmdArgs = append(cmdArgs, "have "+h.String())
232		}
233		cmdArgs = append(cmdArgs, "done")
234	
235		body, err := EncodeCommand("fetch", caps.RequestCapabilities(), cmdArgs)
236		if err != nil {
237			return nil, err
238		}
239		reader, err := PostRPCStream(ctx, conn, transport.UploadPackService, body, true, "upload-pack fetch")
240		if err != nil {
241			return nil, err
242		}
243		packStream, err := openV2PackStream(reader, verbose)
244		if err != nil {
245			_ = reader.Close()
246			return nil, err
247		}
248		return packStream, nil
249	}

  "new_string": "// sessionStderr is an io.Writer that hands writes to the live progress\n// reporter when one is attached to the syncSession, so verbose slog\n// lines and server-side sideband progress (\"Resolving deltas …\") land\n// above the in-place ticker frame instead of clobbering it. Falls back\n// to os.Stderr when no reporter is active.\n//\n// Each Write may carry multiple lines or carriage-returned in-place\n// updates; both '\\n' and '\\r' are treated as line ends so the reporter\n// receives one notify per logical line.\ntype sessionStderr struct{ s *syncSession }\n\nfunc (w sessionStderr) Write(b []byte) (int, error) {\n\tif w.s == nil || w.s.progress == nil {\n\t\tn, err := os.Stderr.Write(b)\n\t\tif err != nil {\n\t\t\treturn n, fmt.Errorf(\"stderr write: %w\", err)\n\t\t}\n\t\treturn n, nil\n\t}\n\ts := string(b)\n\tfor s != \"\" {\n\t\ti := strings.IndexAny(s, \"\\r\\n\")\n\t\tif i < 0 {\n\t\t\tw.s.progress.notify(s)\n\t\t\tbreak\n\t\t}\n\t\tif i > 0 {\n\t\t\tw.s.progress.notify(s[:i])\n\t\t}\n\t\ts = s[i+1:]\n\t}\n\treturn len(b), nil\n}\n\n// stderrIsTTY reports whether stderr is attached to a terminal. The\n// progress ticker is suppressed otherwise because '\\r' updates only make\n// sense on a TTY and would otherwise spam log files.\nfunc stderrIsTTY() bool {"

Returns (nil, nil) when subdivided (caller\n// should continue to retry), or (prepended reader, nil) to proceed with push.\nfunc checkPackSizeAndSubdivide(\n\tr io.ReadCloser,\n\tbatchLimit int64,\n\tsubdivide func(estimatedBytes int64) bool,\n) (io.ReadCloser, error) { //nolint:unparam // error return kept for future use\n\tvar header [12]byte\n\tn, err := io.ReadFull(r, header[:])\n\tif err != nil {\n\t\t// Short pack or error — let the push handle it\n\t\tprefixed := io.MultiReader(bytes.NewReader(header[:n]), r)\n\t\treturn &wrappedMultiRC{Reader: prefixed, Closer: r}, nil //nolint:nilerr // below threshold is not an error, we return the original reader\n\t}\n\tif string(header[:4]) != \"PACK\" {\n\t\t// Not a standard packfile — can't estimate, proceed\n\t\tprefixed := io.MultiReader(bytes.NewReader(header[:]), r)\n\t\treturn &wrappedMultiRC{Reader: prefixed, Closer: r}, nil\n\t}\n\tobjectCount := int64(header[8])<<24 | int64(header[9])<<16 | int64(header[10])<<8 | int64(header[11])\n\testimated := objectCount * estimatedBytesPerObject\n\n\tif estimated > batchLimit && subdivide(estimated) {\n\t\t_ = r.Close()\n\t\treturn nil, nil //nolint:nilnil // nil reader signals no subdivision needed\n\t}\n\n\tprefixed := io.MultiReader(bytes.NewReader(header[:]), r)\n\treturn &wrappedMultiRC{Reader: prefixed, Closer: r}, nil\n}",
  "new_string": "// checkPackSizeAndSubdivide reads the 12-byte PACK header to get the object\n// count, estimates total pack size, and if it exceeds batchLimit, closes the\n// reader and calls subdivide() with the estimate so the caller can include\n// it in user-facing messages. Returns (nil, estimate, nil) when subdivided,\n// or (prepended reader, estimate, nil) to proceed with push. Estimate is 0\n// when the header could not be read or the body is not a PACK.\nfunc checkPackSizeAndSubdivide(\n\tr io.ReadCloser,\n\tbatchLimit int64,\n\tsubdivide func(estimatedBytes int64) bool,\n) (io.ReadCloser, int64, error) { //nolint:unparam // error return kept for future use\n\tvar header [12]byte\n\tn, err := io.ReadFull(r, header[:])\n\tif err != nil {\n\t\t// Short pack or error — let the push handle it\n\t\tprefixed := io.MultiReader(bytes.NewReader(header[:n]), r)\n\t\treturn &wrappedMultiRC{Reader: prefixed, Closer: r}, 0, nil //nolint:nilerr // below threshold is not an error, we return the original reader\n\t}\n\tif string(header[:4]) != \"PACK\" {\n\t\t// Not a standard packfile — can't estimate, proceed\n\t\tprefixed := io.MultiReader(bytes.NewReader(header[:]), r)\n\t\treturn &wrappedMultiRC{Reader: prefixed, Closer: r}, 0, nil\n\t}\n\tobjectCount := int64(header[8])<<24 | int64(header[9])<<16 | int64(header[10])<<8 | int64(header[11])\n\testimated := objectCount * estimatedBytesPerObject\n\n\tif estimated > batchLimit && subdivide(estimated) {\n\t\t_ = r.Close()\n\t\treturn nil, estimated, nil //nolint:nilnil // nil reader signals no subdivision needed\n\t}\n\n\tprefixed := io.MultiReader(bytes.NewReader(header[:]), r)\n\treturn &wrappedMultiRC{Reader: prefixed, Closer: r}, estimated, nil\n}"
}

> AGENT

Both shipped:

**`52d3f19`** — `--verbose` + `--progress` no longer fight for stderr. The slog handler and go-git's sideband progress sink (the `source: Enumerating objects…` lines) both write through a `sessionStderr` that routes via `progressReporter.notify()` when the ticker is active — clearing the frame, printing the line, re-drawing on the next tick. Both `\n` and `\r` are treated as line ends so `Compressing 36%\rCompressing 50%\rCompressing 100%` becomes three clean lines above the ticker instead of clobbering it.

**`4a759ed`** — Two new verbose log lines that answer your earlier diagnostic question:

```
level=INFO msg="bootstrap batch push attempting" branch=... batch=1 batch_total=4 estimated_bytes=187654000 target_limit_bytes=268435456
level=INFO msg="bootstrap batch push failed" branch=... batch=1 estimated_bytes=187654000 target_limit_bytes=268435456 will_subdivide=false error="target receive-pack: http 500: ... Internal Server Error"
```

If `will_subdivide=false` on the failed line and `estimated_bytes` is well under `target_limit_bytes`, the 500 isn't a body-size issue. If it's right at the boundary, Cloudflare is probably masking body-size as 500 and we should widen the heuristic. Re-run with `--verbose --progress` and the trajectory will be there to inspect.

github.com → 1.96 GB @ 5.07 MB/s  │  1.96 GB @ 5.06 MB/s → 8b04592ed74a5cc…cloudflare.net  (pack 1/4)time=2026-05-04T19:33:03.451+02:00 level=INFO msg="bootstrap batch subdividing after target size rejection" branch=refs/heads/entire/checkpoints/v1 old_remaining=4 new_remaining=8 error="target receive-pack: http 413: https://8b04592ed74a5cce30d355b07276caf3.artifacts.cloudflare.net/git/soph/test-repo-bench1.git/git-receive-pack [Cf-Ray=9f693d41afacd2af-FRA, Server=cloudflare, Content-Type=text/html; charset=UTF-8] <html>\r\n<head><title>413 Payload Too Large</title></head>\r\n<body>\r\n<center><h1>413 Payload Too Large</h1></center>\r\n<hr><center>cloudflare</center>\r\n</body>\r\n</html>"

> AGENT

That's still showing collision — likely my clear-via-spaces approach isn't covering the line fully on your terminal width. The fix: use ANSI's "erase entire line" escape (`\x1b[2K`) instead of overwriting with bytes' worth of spaces. That guarantees the line is cleared regardless of UTF-8 byte/column mismatch (your line has 4 multi-byte chars, so byte-length is ~8 wider than display width — spaces overshoot the cursor and may wrap awkwardly).

> AGENT

Re-run with `--verbose --progress` and the slog/notice lines should now land cleanly on their own row above the ticker. The ticker's `\r\x1b[2K` clears the entire previous row before drawing each frame, and notify does the same before printing a one-time message — so multi-byte UTF-8 in the progress line can no longer bleed through.

If you still see overlap after this, it's almost certainly your terminal not honoring `\x1b[2K` — but every modern macOS terminal (Terminal.app, iTerm2, alacritty, Ghostty, kitty, WezTerm) supports it, so this should be it.

The new bug: `source: ` gets split onto its own line because `prefixedLineWriter` calls `sessionStderr.Write` *twice* per logical line — once with the prefix and once with the content+terminator. Our writer notifies each Write as a separate line. I need to buffer partial lines until a terminator arrives.

This matters for prefixedLineWriter, which writes a logical\n// line in two calls — first the prefix (\"source: \"), then the content\n// with terminator — and would otherwise produce two separate notify\n// frames split mid-line. > AGENT

Re-run with `--verbose --progress` and the sideband progress should now read as proper single-row updates (`source: Counting objects: 10% (43/426)`) instead of the prefix being broken onto its own row.

Quick caveat to flag: even with this fix, server-side progress at high frequency (the percentage updates every few hundred ms) will scroll past pretty fast under `--verbose`. If the noise is too much in practice, there are two simple follow-ups:
1. Throttle the sideband sink so we don't pass every 1% update through (drop frames within e.g. 250ms of the previous one).
2. Send sideband progress through `notify` only when it differs from the previous frame (skip duplicates).

Mention if either becomes annoying in real use.

> AGENT

Yes — that's git's natural sideband behavior with `\r` for in-place updates. We're currently inserting `\n` for both, which scrolls. Fix: split a 2-row live region — sideband progress as a "transient" row above the throughput ticker, and emit `\n` only for permanent lines (slog, notices). Sideband `\r` updates rewrite the transient row in place.

It is intentionally a one-line in-place renderer so it\n// stays out of the way of the final command output.\ntype progressReporter struct {\n\tout      io.Writer\n\tstats    *statsCollector\n\tinterval time.Duration\n\tstart    time.Time\n\n\tstopOnce sync.Once\n\tstop     chan struct{}\n\tdone     chan struct{}\n\n\tmu      sync.Mutex\n\tlastLen int\n}",
  "new_string": "// progressReporter renders live per-side throughput to a writer (typically\n// os.Stderr) by sampling the statsCollector's atomic byte counters on a\n// fixed interval.\n//\n// The visible region is at most two rows: an optional \"transient\" line\n// above (used for in-place sideband progress like \"source: Compressing\n// objects: 89%\") and the throughput ticker below. Each redraw uses\n// cursor-up + erase-to-end-of-screen to overwrite the whole region in\n// place, so '\\r'-terminated sideband updates from go-git read as a\n// single updating row instead of scrolling line by line.\ntype progressReporter struct {\n\tout      io.Writer\n\tstats    *statsCollector\n\tinterval time.Duration\n\tstart    time.Time\n\n\tstopOnce sync.Once\n\tstop     chan struct{}\n\tdone     chan struct{}\n\n\tmu        sync.Mutex\n\trowsDrawn int    // rows currently occupying the live region\n\tlastLine  string // last progress line, kept so setTransient can redraw without re-sampling\n\ttransient string // current sideband-progress line, \"\" when none\n}"
}

Used in place of a\n// run of N spaces because tracked byte length doesn't match display\n// width when the progress line contains multi-byte UTF-8 (→, │, …);\n// overshooting with spaces can wrap and leave residue on the next row.\nconst clearLine = \"\\r\\x1b[2K\"\n\n// notify writes a one-time message above the live progress line. The\n// current frame is cleared first so the message lands on a clean row,\n// and lastLen is reset so the next tick redraws the progress below.\n// Safe to call from any goroutine, including while the ticker is\n// running.\nfunc (p *progressReporter) notify(msg string) {\n\tp.mu.Lock()\n\tdefer p.mu.Unlock()\n\tif p.lastLen > 0 {\n\t\tfmt.Fprint(p.out, clearLine)\n\t}\n\tfmt.Fprintln(p.out, msg)\n\tp.lastLen = 0\n}\n\n// terminate halts the ticker, draws one final frame so the printed line\n// reflects the closing byte counts, and emits a newline so subsequent\n// command output starts on a fresh row.\nfunc (p *progressReporter) terminate() {\n\tp.stopOnce.Do(func() {\n\t\tclose(p.stop)\n\t\t<-p.done\n\t\tp.render(true)\n\t\tp.mu.Lock()\n\t\tif p.lastLen > 0 {\n\t\t\tfmt.Fprintln(p.out)\n\t\t}\n\t\tp.mu.Unlock()\n\t})\n}\n\nfunc (p *progressReporter) render(final bool) {\n\tsides := p.stats.liveSides()\n\tif len(sides) == 0 && !final {\n\t\treturn\n\t}\n\tsort.Slice(sides, func(i, j int) bool { return sides[i].Label < sides[j].Label })\n\telapsed := time.Since(p.start)\n\n\tvar b strings.Builder\n\tfor i, side := range sides {\n\t\tif i > 0 {\n\t\t\tb.WriteString(sideSeparator)\n\t\t}\n\t\tb.WriteString(formatSide(side, elapsed, final))\n\t}\n\t// Surface the current activity label (e.g. \"pack 3/8\") on live\n\t// frames only. The final frame is implicitly \"done\" — appending\n\t// the last in-progress phase there would read as still-running.\n\tif !final {\n\t\tif phase := p.stats.getPhase(); phase != \"\" {\n\t\t\tb.WriteString(\"  (\")\n\t\t\tb.WriteString(phase)\n\t\t\tb.WriteString(\")\")\n\t\t}\n\t}\n\tline := b.String()\n\n\tp.mu.Lock()\n\tdefer p.mu.Unlock()\n\tfmt.Fprint(p.out, clearLine+line)\n\tp.lastLen = len(line)\n}",
  "new_string": "// ANSI control sequences we use to redraw the live region in place.\n// 2K erases the entire current line; J erases from the cursor to the\n// end of the screen (covers both rows when the transient is shown);\n// %dA moves the cursor up that many lines. All are widely supported.\nconst (\n\tclearLine = \"\\r\\x1b[2K\"\n\tclearDown = \"\\x1b[J\"\n)\n\n// cursorUpToTopLocked positions the cursor at column 0 of the top row\n// of the currently-drawn live region. Caller must hold p.mu.\nfunc (p *progressReporter) cursorUpToTopLocked() {\n\tif p.rowsDrawn <= 1 {\n\t\tfmt.Fprint(p.out, \"\\r\")\n\t\treturn\n\t}\n\tfmt.Fprintf(p.out, \"\\x1b[%dA\\r\", p.rowsDrawn-1)\n}\n\n// drawLocked rewrites the live region in place: cursor jumps to the top\n// row, erases everything below, then writes transient (if any) followed\n// by the throughput line. Cursor is left at the end of the throughput\n// row so subsequent ticker frames see rowsDrawn=region-height.\nfunc (p *progressReporter) drawLocked(line string) {\n\tif p.rowsDrawn > 0 {\n\t\tp.cursorUpToTopLocked()\n\t}\n\tfmt.Fprint(p.out, clearDown)\n\n\trows := 0\n\tif p.transient != \"\" {\n\t\tfmt.Fprintln(p.out, p.transient)\n\t\trows++\n\t}\n\tif line != \"\" {\n\t\tfmt.Fprint(p.out, line)\n\t\trows++\n\t}\n\tp.rowsDrawn = rows\n\tp.lastLine = line\n}\n\n// notify writes a one-time permanent message above the live region.\n// The region is cleared first so the message lands on a clean row, and\n// rowsDrawn is reset so the next render redraws transient + ticker\n// below. Safe to call concurrently with the ticker.\nfunc (p *progressReporter) notify(msg string) {\n\tp.mu.Lock()\n\tdefer p.mu.Unlock()\n\tif p.rowsDrawn > 0 {\n\t\tp.cursorUpToTopLocked()\n\t\tfmt.Fprint(p.out, clearDown)\n\t}\n\tfmt.Fprintln(p.out, msg)\n\tp.rowsDrawn = 0\n}\n\n// setTransient updates the in-place sideband row above the ticker.\n// Pass \"\" to clear it. Triggers an immediate redraw so '\\r'-driven\n// progress (Compressing/Counting/Resolving) feels responsive between\n// ticker intervals.\nfunc (p *progressReporter) setTransient(line string) {\n\tp.mu.Lock()\n\tdefer p.mu.Unlock()\n\tp.transient = line\n\tp.drawLocked(p.lastLine)\n}\n\n// terminate halts the ticker, draws one final frame so the printed line\n// reflects the closing byte counts, and emits a newline so subsequent\n// command output starts on a fresh row.\nfunc (p *progressReporter) terminate() {\n\tp.stopOnce.Do(func() {\n\t\tclose(p.stop)\n\t\t<-p.done\n\t\tp.render(true)\n\t\tp.mu.Lock()\n\t\tif p.rowsDrawn > 0 {\n\t\t\tfmt.Fprintln(p.out)\n\t\t}\n\t\tp.mu.Unlock()\n\t})\n}\n\nfunc (p *progressReporter) render(final bool) {\n\tsides := p.stats.liveSides()\n\tif len(sides) == 0 && !final {\n\t\treturn\n\t}\n\tsort.Slice(sides, func(i, j int) bool { return sides[i].Label < sides[j].Label })\n\telapsed := time.Since(p.start)\n\n\tvar b strings.Builder\n\tfor i, side := range sides {\n\t\tif i > 0 {\n\t\t\tb.WriteString(sideSeparator)\n\t\t}\n\t\tb.WriteString(formatSide(side, elapsed, final))\n\t}\n\t// Surface the current activity label (e.g. \"pack 3/8\") on live\n\t// frames only. The final frame is implicitly \"done\" — appending\n\t// the last in-progress phase there would read as still-running.\n\tif !final {\n\t\tif phase := p.stats.getPhase(); phase != \"\" {\n\t\t\tb.WriteString(\"  (\")\n\t\t\tb.WriteString(phase)\n\t\t\tb.WriteString(\")\")\n\t\t}\n\t}\n\tline := b.String()\n\n\tp.mu.Lock()\n\tdefer p.mu.Unlock()\n\tp.drawLocked(line)\n}"
}

Re-run with `--verbose --progress` and you'll see:

```
time=… INFO bootstrap fetching refs from source        ← scrolls (permanent)
time=… INFO bootstrap pushing refs to target           ← scrolls (permanent)
source: Compressing objects:  89% (263/295)            ← in-place update on this single row
github.com → 1.6 GB @ 5 MB/s  │  … → cloudflare.net  (pack 1/4)   ← in-place ticker below
```

When the sideband phase finishes (`Compressing 100%, done.\n`), that line scrolls into the permanent log above and the transient row goes empty until the next phase starts (e.g., `Resolving deltas:`). The throughput ticker keeps running on its own row underneath the whole time.

Caveat: this only works on terminals that honor `\x1b[%dA` (cursor-up) and `\x1b[J` (erase-to-end-of-screen) — that's every modern macOS/Linux/Windows terminal but no-op pipes/log files (which we already auto-suppress via the TTY check, so no change there).

> AGENT

Good question — and the short answer is: plain `git push --mirror` would absolutely hit the same 413, because git itself does not auto-subdivide packfiles. There's no native fallback to "split into smaller packs and push them sequentially" — that incremental-checkpoint behavior is exactly the value-add git-sync's batched bootstrap is providing.

What `http.postBuffer` does *not* do, despite the common belief: it's just a local memory buffer for the request body. Bumping it lets git send a larger pack in one POST, but it doesn't chunk to fit a server limit. If the pack exceeds Cloudflare's body cap, git push fails with 413 and stops.

To verify and study the handshake, the relevant env vars on git CLI are:

```bash
GIT_TRACE=1                    # high-level git operations
GIT_TRACE_CURL=1               # full HTTP request/response, headers + first ~4 KB body
GIT_TRACE_CURL_NO_DATA=1       # same as above but suppresses request bodies (less noise)
GIT_TRACE_PACKET=1             # pkt-line level (sees protocol v2 commands, sideband framing)
GIT_TRACE_PACKFILE=/tmp/pack   # writes the negotiated pack to a file for inspection
```

So a useful comparison run would be:

```bash
GIT_TRACE=1 GIT_TRACE_CURL=1 git push --mirror --progress \
  https://8b04592e…cloudflare.net/git/soph/test-repo-bench1.git
```

You'll see:
1. the `info/refs?service=git-receive-pack` GET with caps advertised back
2. the single `git-receive-pack` POST containing the full pack
3. on a sufficiently large repo, the response will be `HTTP/1.1 413 Payload Too Large` and git will just exit non-zero — no retry logic kicks in

If you want to confirm the body-size threshold is identical to what git-sync hit, the `GIT_TRACE_CURL=1` output shows `Content-Length: …` on the POST. Compare that to the `target_limit_bytes` that git-sync logged. If they match (or git's number is just over Cloudflare's parsed limit), it's the same wall.

If you do want to know where Cloudflare's actual cap is to set `--target-max-pack-bytes` upfront (skipping the 1 → 2 → 4 → … 32 dance), running `GIT_TRACE_CURL=1 git push --mirror …` once and grepping the failure response for the limit, or pulling the parsed limit out of git-sync's `target_limit_bytes` log line on the first 413, both work. Then `git-sync sync --target-max-pack-bytes 50000000` (or whatever the cap is) will start at the right size on the next run.

> AGENT

That's the binary packfile body. Suppress it with `GIT_TRACE_CURL_NO_DATA=1` — keeps every header line and protocol message but drops the body dumps:

```bash
GIT_TRACE=1 GIT_TRACE_CURL=1 GIT_TRACE_CURL_NO_DATA=1 \
  git push --mirror --progress \
  https://8b04592e…cloudflare.net/git/soph/test-repo-bench1.git
```

You'll still see the `=> Send header: …` lines (request method, URL, content-type, content-length) and `<= Recv header: …` (status code, response headers), but `=> Send data:` blobs become `=> Send data, NNNN bytes (0xXXXX)` size-only stubs. That's exactly the level you need for the handshake — which capabilities both sides advertised, what content-length actually went up, what status code came back.

If you want to dump the response body but not the request body (so you can read Cloudflare's HTML 413 explanation without the gigabyte of pack going up), there isn't a separate flag for that — `GIT_TRACE_CURL_NO_DATA=1` suppresses both directions. But the response is small enough that even with `GIT_TRACE_CURL=1` and no `_NO_DATA`, the `<= Recv data:` for a 413 is tiny; the noise is all on the upload side. So the practical workflow is:

- First run: `GIT_TRACE_CURL_NO_DATA=1` to see headers
- If you want the response body too: `tee` the entire trace and grep for `<= Recv` lines after the fact

> AGENT

Perfect — this is exactly the data point we needed. Three concrete things from that trace:

1. **Cloudflare's actual cap is ~500 MiB**, not 512. Look at this line:
   ```
   == Info: abort upload after having sent 524576868 bytes
   ```
   That's 524,576,868 bytes ≈ 500.27 MiB. Cloudflare cuts the request mid-upload (sends the 413 response before git is done writing) right around the 500 MiB mark. git-sync's default `defaultTargetMaxPackBytes = 512 MiB` is *just* over that wall, which is why batched mode still hits 413 once and has to split 1 → 2 → 4 → … the first time.

2. **Plain `git push --mirror` is dead in the water at this point.** No retry, no chunking, no fallback — just `error: RPC failed; HTTP 413` and `fatal: the remote end hung up unexpectedly`. The "Everything up-to-date" line at the bottom is a quirk of git-push's exit handling, not a success. So git-sync's incremental checkpoint behavior really is what's making this repo syncable at all to this endpoint.

3. **No Cloudflare-specific size header in the response** — just `HTTP/2 413` and a 167-byte HTML body. There's nothing in the headers we could parse to learn the cap programmatically; we'd need a hardcoded heuristic or trial-and-error.

So the immediate practical fix for your re-runs: pass `--target-max-pack-bytes` upfront and skip the dance entirely. Two reasonable values:

```bash
# Exactly 500 MiB — matches the observed cap, may still fail near the boundary
git-sync sync --target-max-pack-bytes 524288000 …

# 450 MiB — safer margin, succeeds on first batched attempt
git-sync sync --target-max-pack-bytes 471859200 …
```

If you want a small follow-up code change: bump `defaultTargetMaxPackBytes` in `internal/strategy/bootstrap/bootstrap.go` from `512 * 1024 * 1024` to `480 * 1024 * 1024` (480 MiB). That gives a safety margin against the Cloudflare wall and will succeed on the first batched attempt for everyone, not just you. The constant is already a "best-guess fallback" used only when we can't parse the limit from the error — which is exactly Cloudflare's case. Want me to land that?

Your live counter shows ~78 MB and rising, so reality is roughly 60% larger than the heuristic — typical for repos with large blobs.
- **`target_limit_bytes=524288000`** = the 500 MiB you passed via `--target-max-pack-bytes`.
- **`batch_total=1`** means the planner calculated *one* checkpoint will fit. With ~78 MB actual vs a 500 MiB limit, you have ~6× headroom — well within the wall, so a single pack is correct here.

The 1 → 2 → 4 → … → 32 dance you saw earlier was for `cli.git`, which has a real pack around 960 MiB (you can see this in your earlier `git push --mirror` trace: `Writing objects: 100% (64686/64686), 960.23 MiB`). With a 500 MiB cap, that needs ~2 chunks at minimum — but because the planner's *first* estimate undershot real bytes (per-object × 750 said ~48 MB but reality was ~960 MB), it planned 1 pack, fetched it, peeked the header → estimate said 48 MB → tried to push → 413 from Cloudflare at 524 MB → subdivide 1→2 → re-fetch each half → still over → subdivide 2→4 → ... until each piece was small enough to slip under 500 MiB. That's the dance.

For the current repo, you're done at `pack 1/1`. If the actual push completes around 78 MB without a 413, that confirms it.

If you want to make the planner's first estimate much closer to truth (and avoid the dance for `cli.git`-shaped repos), we could:

1. **Bump `estimatedBytesPerObject` from 750 → ~1500** to be more conservative for blob-heavy repos. Trade-off: skinny repos plan more chunks than needed (cheap; extra batches finish fast).
2. **Or sample the actual pack size on a probe fetch first** before committing to a chunk count. Heavier — adds a roundtrip — but precise.

OK that changes the picture — same repo for everything, so the dance was on this one too. You're right that `batch_total=1` is misleading. Here's what's actually happening:

**The heuristic is wildly wrong for this repo.** Real numbers:
- Actual pack size (from your `git push --mirror` trace): 960.23 MiB ≈ 1,006 MB
- Object count: 64,686
- Real bytes/object: ~15,562
- Our hardcoded estimate (`estimatedBytesPerObject = 750`): **20× too low**

So the planner does this:
1. `estimateBatchCount(chainLen, 524 MB)` says "1 batch is fine" because chain × 65 KiB/commit < 524 MB
2. After fetching, header peek says `48 MB` (`64,686 × 750`) → "definitely fine, push it"
3. Cloudflare's actual cut is around 524 MB; real pack is ~960 MB → **413**
4. Post-rejection subdivide *halves*: `1 → 2`. Re-fetch each half, header still says ~24 MB, push, fail again.
5. Repeat: `2 → 4 → 8 → 16 → 32`. Each iteration also re-fetches the full chain from source.

Setting `--target-max-pack-bytes 524288000` didn't avoid the dance — it just set the limit. The dance is driven by reactive halving on a too-optimistic estimate.

The real fix: **use actual data from the failed push to subdivide intelligently.** We already have it — the target-side byte counter tells us exactly how many bytes were transmitted before Cloudflare cut us off. If 524 MB went up before the 413 and the limit is 500 MB, and we know there are N more checkpoints remaining, we can compute the *real* needed pack count in one step:

```
neededPacks = ceil(real_bytes_sent / target_limit × safety_margin)
```

Jump straight from 1 → 32 (or whatever the actual ratio demands) on the first 413, instead of dancing for log₂(32) = 5 rounds. That's 5 wasted source re-fetches per branch.

Two options for the fix:

1. **Smart subdivision from observed pack size** — adds ~30 lines to the post-rejection branch. Snapshot `target.bytes` before `PushPack`, compute the delta on failure, divide remaining by `(delta / limit)`. One-shot jump to the right count.

2. **Cheaper alternative**: just bump `estimatedBytesPerObject` from 750 → ~3000 (4× more conservative). Pre-flight check would catch the fat pack and subdivide pre-push without the wasted upload. Skinny repos plan a few extra batches, harmless. Doesn't solve every case but handles the common "blob-heavy" failure mode without code complexity.

700	// subdivideCheckpoints splits each remaining checkpoint range in half using
701	// the full commit chain. Called when a batch push is rejected for exceeding
702	// the target's body-size limit. Returns the expanded checkpoint list; if no
703	// split is possible (ranges are already 1 commit), returns the input unchanged.
704	func subdivideCheckpoints(chain []plumbing.Hash, current plumbing.Hash, remaining []plumbing.Hash) []plumbing.Hash {
705		chainIdx := make(map[plumbing.Hash]int, len(chain))
706		for i, h := range chain {
707			chainIdx[h] = i
708		}
709		curIdx, ok := chainIdx[current]
710		if !ok && !current.IsZero() {
711			return remaining
712		}
713		if current.IsZero() {
714			curIdx = -1
715		}
716	
717		expanded := make([]plumbing.Hash, 0, len(remaining)*2)
718		prev := curIdx
719		for _, cp := range remaining {
720			cpIdx, ok := chainIdx[cp]
721			if !ok {
722				expanded = append(expanded, cp)
723				continue
724			}
725			gap := cpIdx - prev
726			if gap > 1 {
727				midIdx := prev + gap/2
728				expanded = append(expanded, chain[midIdx])
729			}
730			expanded = append(expanded, cp)
731			prev = cpIdx
732		}
733		return expanded
734	}
735	
736	func evenCheckpoints(chain []plumbing.Hash, numBatches int) []plumbing.Hash {
737		if numBatches <= 1 || len(chain) <= 1 || numBatches >= len(chain) {
738			return []plumbing.Hash{chain[len(chain)-1]}
739		}
740		checkpoints := make([]plumbing.Hash, 0, numBatches)
741		batchSize := len(chain) / numBatches
742		for i := range numBatches - 1 {
743			idx := (i+1)*batchSize - 1
744			if idx >= len(chain)-1 {
745				break
746			}
747			checkpoints = append(checkpoints, chain[idx])
748		}
749		checkpoints = append(checkpoints, chain[len(chain)-1])
750		return checkpoints
751	}

Both branches pushed:

- **`soph/progress-indicators`** (12 commits, off `main`) → https://github.com/entireio/git-sync/pull/new/soph/progress-indicators
- **`soph/smart-subdivision`** (1 commit, off `main`) → https://github.com/entireio/git-sync/pull/new/soph/smart-subdivision

Once you've opened the PR for smart-subdivision, ping me and I'll rebase progress-indicators on top of it. If you want, I can do the rebase now anyway — it's two independent commit ranges with no overlap, so it should be a clean rebase regardless of merge order.

Quick recap of what's in the smart-subdivision commit:

- `packReadCounter` wraps the pack stream; `counter.n` reports bytes the HTTP transport actually pulled before the server returned 413.
- `observedSubdivisionFactor(sent, limit)` returns `ceil(sent × 2 / limit)` (minimum 2). The `× 2` is the safety multiplier for the unsent-but-real portion of the pack.
- `subdivideToFactor` keeps halving until the count reaches the requested factor; rounds up to the next power of 2.
- The post-rejection branch in `bootstrap.go` now uses both. For your Cloudflare scenario (524 MiB sent, 500 MiB limit, real pack 960 MiB), factor = 3 → first split jumps 1 → 4 packs, each ~240 MiB, well within the cap. One round instead of five.
- Slog line now carries `sent_bytes`, `limit_bytes`, and `factor` so verbose runs show the arithmetic.

Author: Stefan Haubold <stefan@entire.io>
Date:   Mon May 4 21:17:56 2026 +0200

    Use observed pack size to size post-rejection subdivisions
    
    Bootstrap's batched-mode subdivide path was always halving the
    remaining checkpoint count when a target rejected a pack with
    HTTP 413. For a repo whose real per-object byte size is far above
    the per-object heuristic (estimatedBytesPerObject = 750), this
    forces a long dance: 1 → 2 → 4 → 8 → 16 → 32 sub-packs across five
    rejected pushes, each preceded by a fresh source fetch. For a
    ~960 MiB pack against Cloudflare's ~500 MiB body cap, that's five
    wasted ~500 MiB uploads.
    
    Wrap the pack reader handed to PushPack in a packReadCounter so the
    loop learns how many bytes actually went up before the cutoff,
    then use observed bytes ÷ target limit (× 2 safety multiplier) to
    choose the new sub-pack count in one informed jump. The Cloudflare
    case folds from five rounds into a single 1 → 4 split.
    
    Falls back to the existing halving behaviour when the signal is
    missing (sentBytes ≤ 0 or limit ≤ 0). Surfaces sent_bytes,
    limit_bytes, and computed factor in the slog line so verbose runs
    show the math.

Done. Layout now:

- **`main`** (752b6e3)
- **`soph/smart-subdivision`** (1 commit: `f794e73`) — base for the next stack
- **`soph/progress-indicators`** (12 commits, rebased on top of smart-subdivision) — head is now `2cd03f6`

Everything builds, tests pass with `-race`, lint clean. Three conflicts resolved during the rebase, all in `bootstrap.go` around the post-rejection subdivide block — each resolution kept smart-subdivision's structure (`pushErr` variable, factor-based splitting, the `sent_bytes` / `limit_bytes` / `factor` slog fields) and folded in the progress branch's additions (the `notice()` call, the `bootstrap batch push failed` log line, the limit-text in the user-facing notice). The `bootstrap batch push failed` log now also carries `sent_bytes` since that's available now — useful diagnostic when verifying the smart-subdivision math in a real run.

> DEVELOPER

Subdivision skipped when factor ≤ remaining checkpoint count

High Severity

subdivideToFactor uses len(expanded) < targetCount as its loop guard, so when the remaining checkpoint count already meets or exceeds factor, it returns unchanged. The caller then checks len(expanded) > len(batch.Checkpoints[idx:]), which evaluates to false, turning a recoverable 413 into a hard failure. This is a regression from the old code, which always called subdivideCheckpoints at least once. When a reverse proxy cuts the connection at its body limit, sentBytes ≈ limit, so factor is always 2. The first rejection subdivides 1→2, but the second rejection sees 2 remaining ≥ factor 2, skips subdivision entirely, and fails.

> AGENT

Good catch — that's a real regression. The old behavior always called `subdivideCheckpoints` once unconditionally; my version returns the input untouched when `len(remaining) >= factor`, which means a 2nd rejection on a 2-piece batch (factor still =2 because `sent ≈ limit`) skips subdivision and turns into a hard fail.

Fix: guarantee at least one subdivision per call. Then keep subdividing while we're still under the requested factor.

Tests + lint clean. Force-pushed.

The fix in one paragraph: `subdivideToFactor` now unconditionally calls `subdivideCheckpoints` once before checking the targetCount loop, so a call with `len(remaining) ≥ targetCount` still produces forward progress instead of returning the input unchanged. The only path that still returns the input is when subdivision is genuinely impossible (every gap is already 1 commit) — guarded by the `len(expanded) <= len(remaining)` check on the first round.

> DEVELOPER

one question: I have a network stats tool on my mac, it instantly says 44MB/s up/down each, but the git-sync out put slowly moves up from 13 to 27 but never gets past that

> AGENT

That's expected behavior — and fixable. The displayed rate is `bytes ÷ (last_byte_time − stats_start_time)`. `stats_start_time` is when the syncer session was created, *before* any bytes flow. So the active window includes the time spent on auth, info-refs, ls-refs, and ref planning — all of which are tiny but slow setup phases. The actual pack streaming happens later, at the wire-rate your network tool sees, but the displayed average dilutes it across the whole session.

Concretely, for a transfer that goes:

- `t = 0–3s`: setup (auth + ref listing, ~hundreds of KB)
- `t = 3–13s`: pack streaming at 44 MB/s, ~440 MB total

At `t=13s` you'd see `441 MB / 13s = 33.9 MB/s` displayed, slowly climbing toward 44 MB/s as the proportion of streaming-time grows but never reaching it. That matches your "13 → 27, never past 27" — the streaming hasn't run long enough yet for the average to converge.

There's also a smaller secondary factor: macOS network tools count wire bytes (TCP/TLS framing, HTTP headers, retransmissions, plus *both* directions on each socket). Our counter wraps the HTTP body, so we miss the framing overhead. That's maybe 5–10% though — not the bulk of your gap.

Two easy fixes, depending on what you want the number to mean:

1. **"Streaming throughput"** — track `firstByteAt` per side and compute rate over `lastByteAt − firstByteAt` instead of `lastByteAt − sessionStart`. Number jumps to roughly the actual pack-streaming rate (within ~10% of the network tool). Stable, no jitter. Trivial change: 1 field on `sideCounter`, 1 line in `Read`, 1 conditional in `liveSides`.

2. **"Instantaneous throughput"** — sliding window of bytes-per-second over the last ~2 seconds. Closer to what the network tool shows and bouncier (you'd see it ramp up and back down as packs flush). More work: ring buffer + sampler.

I'd recommend (1). The "average over the streaming phase" is what most users actually want — stable enough to read, and matches the headline question "how fast was this transfer?". Want me to land it?

> DEVELOPER

how much work is 2?

> AGENT

Maybe 2–3 hours total. Concretely:

**Core mechanics** (~80 LOC):
- Per-side ring buffer of `(timestamp, cumulative_bytes)` samples — fixed size, e.g. 20 slots for a 2-second window at 100 ms cadence
- A sampler goroutine that ticks every 100 ms and snapshots `bytes.Load()` into the ring (decoupled from `Read`, so no hot-path overhead)
- A `windowRate()` helper that returns `(latest_bytes − oldest_bytes_within_window) / window_seconds`

**Wiring** (~40 LOC):
- Add `InstantBytesPerSec int64` to `SideBytes`
- Populate it in `liveSides()` from the ring
- `formatSide` chooses between active-window rate and instant rate (probably show both: "44 MB/s now · 33 MB/s avg")

**Decisions that add scope**:
- *Jitter smoothing*: raw window rate flickers as packs flush in bursts. EWMA dampens that — another ~15 LOC.
- *End-of-transfer behavior*: instant rate naturally drops to 0 once bytes stop, which conflicts with the "✓ frozen rate" we already have. Either freeze the instant rate at the last non-zero value when idle, or hide the instant rate after the side goes idle (and only show frozen average). Another ~10 LOC.
- *Tests*: ring-buffer unit tests + integration test that exercises a synthetic burst → idle → burst sequence to verify both the live rate and the freeze. ~60 LOC.

So realistic total is **150–200 LOC** vs **10–15 LOC** for option (1) — roughly 10× the work for arguably more accurate UX.

My honest take: option (1) is the better default for a one-shot batch sync tool. The user's question after a sync is usually "how fast did that transfer go?" — for which a stable streaming-window average is more readable than a flickering instant rate. Option (2)'s jitter is more useful for tools you watch continuously (curl, rsync). Land (1) now, leave (2) for later if "I want it to match my network monitor live" turns out to be a real recurring desire.

Want me to do (1)? It's a 5-minute change.

159	func (p *progressReporter) render(final bool) {
160		sides := p.stats.liveSides()
161		if len(sides) == 0 && !final {
162			return
163		}
164		sort.Slice(sides, func(i, j int) bool { return sides[i].Label < sides[j].Label })
165		elapsed := time.Since(p.start)
166	
167		var b strings.Builder
168		for i, side := range sides {
169			if i > 0 {
170				b.WriteString(sideSeparator)
171			}
172			b.WriteString(formatSide(side, elapsed, final))
173		}
174		// Surface the current activity label (e.g. "pack 3/8") on live
175		// frames only. The final frame is implicitly "done" — appending
176		// the last in-progress phase there would read as still-running.
177		if !final {
178			if phase := p.stats.getPhase(); phase != "" {
179				b.WriteString("  (")
180				b.WriteString(phase)
181				b.WriteString(")")
182			}
183		}
184		line := b.String()
185	
186		p.mu.Lock()
187		defer p.mu.Unlock()
188		p.drawLocked(line)
189	}
190	
191	const (
192		sideSeparator    = "  │  "
193		flowArrow        = " → "
194		doneMark         = " ✓"
195		maxHostnameWidth = 30
196		idleThreshold    = 750 * time.Millisecond
197	)
198	
199	// formatSide renders a single side as host + bytes + rate, with a flow
200	// arrow positioned to indicate direction: source on the left of its
201	// counter, target on the right of its counter. Sides with neither label
202	// fall back to "name: bytes @ rate".
203	//
204	// The displayed rate is computed against the side's active window
205	// (start → last byte) when known, so once a transfer ends the number
206	// freezes at the actual transfer rate instead of decaying as the wall
207	// clock keeps ticking. forceDone (set on the final render) and a
208	// per-side idle gap >idleThreshold append a "✓" marker.
209	func formatSide(side SideBytes, fallbackDur time.Duration, forceDone bool) string {
210		name := side.Display
211		if name == "" {
212			name = side.Label
213		}
214		name = truncateHost(name, maxHostnameWidth)
215	
216		rateDur := fallbackDur
217		if side.ActiveNanos > 0 {
218			rateDur = time.Duration(side.ActiveNanos)
219		}
220		rate := formatBytes(side.Bytes) + " @ " + formatRate(side.Bytes, rateDur)
221	
222		done := side.Bytes > 0 && (forceDone || time.Duration(side.IdleNanos) >= idleThreshold)
223		if done {
224			rate += doneMark
225		}
226	
227		switch side.Label {
228		case "source":
229			return name + flowArrow + rate
230		case "target":
231			return rate + flowArrow + name
232		default:
233			return name + ": " + rate
234		}
235	}
236	
237	// truncateHost shortens long hostnames while keeping the apex domain
238	// visible. Returns the original string if it already fits within width,
239	// otherwise preserves the trailing two dotted labels (e.g. "cloudflare.net")

> AGENT

Pushed (no force needed since this is a fast-forward). Re-run with `--progress` and the rate displayed during the streaming phase should match what your network tool shows much more closely — it's now `(latest_bytes − oldest_bytes_within_2s_window) / window_duration`, so it converges to the wire rate within ~2 seconds of streaming starting and tracks short-term variation as packs flush.

Behavior summary:

- **Active transfer**: rolling window (instant rate), ticks at 200 ms with a 2 s window
- **Side goes idle for >750 ms** (or final frame): switches to the active-window average and adds the ✓ marker — that's the "how fast was this transfer?" headline you keep in scrollback
- **End-of-run `throughput:` line**: still the active-window average — appropriate for the post-mortem summary

Two caveats to flag, since (2) trades stability for responsiveness:

1. **Jitter**: pack flushes are bursty. You'll see the live number bounce around — typical range is ±20% within the window. If it gets distracting we can layer EWMA smoothing on top (~15 LOC).
2. **Wire-vs-payload gap**: the network monitor still counts TCP/TLS framing and HTTP headers; our counter sees HTTP body bytes. So expect git-sync's number to read maybe 5–10% lower than your monitor even at peak, even though the streaming-phase math is now correct.

> AGENT

The smart subdivision is doing what it's designed to do, but the design itself is leaving signal on the table. Look at this pattern:

| iteration | sent_bytes | factor |
|-----------|-----------|--------|
| 1 pack    | 526 MB    | 3      |
| 4 packs   | 528 MB    | 3      |
| 8 packs   | 528 MB    | 3      |
| 16 packs  | (in flight) | … |

`sent_bytes` is essentially constant at ~528 MB every round. That's because **Cloudflare cuts the connection at its body cap, so what we observe is always ≈ limit, regardless of how big the pack actually is**. With safety multiplier 2, that always yields `ceil(528 × 2 / 500) = 3` — a useless number. We learn nothing across rounds.

The fundamental issue: `sent_bytes ≈ limit` only tells us "the pack is at least limit-sized". The real pack could be 2×, 5×, 20× the limit. Without knowing, halving (`subdivideCheckpoints` doubles count per call) is conservative; combined with `factor=3` it produces 1 → 4 → 8 → 16 → 32 with one round per server rejection.

There's an extra wrinkle: your repo is *blob-heavy in early commits*. Sub-pack 1/4 has 48,115 objects covering 670 commits; sub-pack 1/8 still has 45,345 objects. So early commits are massively heavy and even halving the commit range barely halves the byte size.

Two complementary fixes I'd suggest:

1. **Bump the safety multiplier when `sent_bytes` is at the cap.** If we observe a capped failure (`sent ≈ limit`), the real size is unknown but most likely much bigger. Use 4× instead of 2×, so factor becomes ~5 and we jump 1 → 8 in one round instead of 1 → 4. Saves a round per rejection.

2. **Calibrate `bytesPerObject` from observed data.** After each failure, compute `sent_bytes / pack_object_count` as a lower bound. Use that calibrated ratio (with safety) in the *pre-flight* `checkPackSizeAndSubdivide` so a too-big sub-pack is caught and split *before* upload, not after another wasted ~528 MB transfer. This is what avoids the wasted source fetches.

(1) is a 5-line change. (2) is ~30 LOC. Want me to do both? I'd recommend yes — alone, (1) saves ~1 round; combined with (2) you'd likely converge in 1-2 rounds instead of 5+, and skip the wasted uploads entirely.

651	// (tiny commits in a sparse repo) to ~2 KiB (blob-heavy repos), with most

653	const estimatedBytesPerObject = 750

655	// checkPackSizeAndSubdivide reads the 12-byte PACK header to get the object
656	// count, estimates total pack size, and if it exceeds batchLimit, closes the
657	// reader and calls subdivide(). Returns (nil, nil) when subdivided (caller
658	// should continue to retry), or (prepended reader, nil) to proceed with push.
659	func checkPackSizeAndSubdivide(
660		r io.ReadCloser,
661		batchLimit int64,
662		subdivide func() bool,
663	) (io.ReadCloser, error) { //nolint:unparam // error return kept for future use
664		var header [12]byte
665		n, err := io.ReadFull(r, header[:])
666		if err != nil {
667			// Short pack or error — let the push handle it
668			prefixed := io.MultiReader(bytes.NewReader(header[:n]), r)
669			return &wrappedMultiRC{Reader: prefixed, Closer: r}, nil //nolint:nilerr // below threshold is not an error, we return the original reader
670		}
671		if string(header[:4]) != "PACK" {
672			// Not a standard packfile — can't estimate, proceed
673			prefixed := io.MultiReader(bytes.NewReader(header[:]), r)
674			return &wrappedMultiRC{Reader: prefixed, Closer: r}, nil
675		}
676		objectCount := int64(header[8])<<24 | int64(header[9])<<16 | int64(header[10])<<8 | int64(header[11])
677		estimated := objectCount * estimatedBytesPerObject
678	
679		if estimated > batchLimit && subdivide() {
680			_ = r.Close()
681			return nil, nil //nolint:nilnil // nil reader signals no subdivision needed
682		}
683

io.MultiReader(bytes.NewReader(header[:n]), r)\n\t\treturn &wrappedMultiRC{Reader: prefixed, Closer: r}, 0, nil //nolint:nilerr // below threshold is not an error, we return the original reader\n\t}\n\tif string(header[:4]) != \"PACK\" {\n\t\t// Not a standard packfile — can't estimate, proceed\n\t\tprefixed := io.MultiReader(bytes.NewReader(header[:]), r)\n\t\treturn &wrappedMultiRC{Reader: prefixed, Closer: r}, 0, nil\n\t}\n\tobjectCount := int64(header[8])<<24 | int64(header[9])<<16 | int64(header[10])<<8 | int64(header[11])\n\testimated := objectCount * bytesPerObject\n\n\tif estimated > batchLimit && subdivide() {\n\t\t_ = r.Close()\n\t\treturn nil, objectCount, nil\n\t}\n\n\tprefixed := io.MultiReader(bytes.NewReader(header[:]), r)\n\treturn &wrappedMultiRC{Reader: prefixed, Closer: r}, objectCount, nil\n}\n\n// calibrateBytesPerObject derives a per-object byte estimate from a\n// rejected push's transmitted-bytes lower bound. sentBytes is the\n// amount our request-body counter saw before the server cut us off,\n// which means the true pack size is at least sentBytes — likely more.\n// The 2× safety multiplier projects from observed lower bound to a\n// pessimistic upper bound, so future pre-flight estimates err on the\n// side of subdividing rather than over-shooting and re-paying for the\n// rejected upload.\n//\n// Returns 0 when calibration is not possible (no signal, or the new\n// value would not be an improvement over the current one) so the\n// caller can keep its existing value.\nfunc calibrateBytesPerObject(sentBytes, objectCount, current int64) int64 {\n\tif sentBytes <= 0 || objectCount <= 0 {\n\t\treturn 0\n\t}\n\tconst safetyMultiplier = 2\n\tcalibrated := safetyMultiplier * sentBytes / objectCount\n\tif calibrated <= current {\n\t\treturn 0\n\t}\n\treturn calibrated\n}"
}

{
  "command": "git add -A && git commit --amend -m \"$(cat <<'EOF'\nUse observed pack size to size post-rejection subdivisions\n\nBootstrap's batched-mode subdivide path was always halving the\nremaining checkpoint count when a target rejected a pack with\nHTTP 413. For a repo whose real per-object byte size is far above\nthe per-object heuristic (estimatedBytesPerObject = 750), this\nforces a long dance: 1 → 2 → 4 → 8 → 16 → 32 sub-packs across five\nrejected pushes, each preceded by a fresh source fetch. For a\n~960 MiB pack against Cloudflare's ~500 MiB body cap, that's five\nwasted ~500 MiB uploads.\n\nWrap the pack reader handed to PushPack in a packReadCounter so the\nloop learns how many bytes actually went up before the cutoff and\nsizes the next attempt accordingly. Three cooperating pieces:\n\n1. observedSubdivisionFactor uses bytes_sent ÷ limit (with safety\n   multiplier) to choose how many sub-packs to split into. When\n   sent_bytes ≈ limit (server cut us off mid-stream — the common\n   reverse-proxy 413 case), the true pack size is unknown but\n   likely much larger than the cap, so the multiplier escalates to\n   4× to converge in a single round. Otherwise 2× is enough.\n\n2. subdivideToFactor halves at least once per call and keeps going\n   while count < target. The unconditional first round matters\n   when factor ≤ remaining: each surviving range may still\n   over-shoot so always making forward progress prevents a hard\n   failure on repeated 413s with sent_bytes ≈ limit.\n\n3. checkPackSizeAndSubdivide now takes a calibrated bytesPerObject\n   instead of using the static 750-byte default. After each 413,\n   calibrateBytesPerObject derives 2 × sent_bytes ÷ pack_objects\n   as a pessimistic upper bound and ratchets the running estimate\n   up. Subsequent sub-packs are pre-emptively split when the\n   calibrated estimate exceeds the limit — saving an entire\n   ~limit-sized wasted upload on blob-heavy repos where the\n   default ratio is 10–20× too low.\n\nFalls back to the legacy halving behaviour when no signal is\navailable (sentBytes ≤ 0 or limit ≤ 0). Surfaces sent_bytes,\nlimit_bytes, factor, and calibrated_bytes_per_object in the slog\noutput so verbose runs show the math.\nEOF\n)\" 2>&1 | tail -3",
  "description": "Amend smart-subdivision with fixes 1+2"
}
